messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard error of the sample mean (under the null)**  

The “standard deviation of the null‑hypothesis test” is usually interpreted as the standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean when the null hypothesis is true.  
It is calculated as:

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

where  
* \(s = 1.4\) (sample standard deviation)  
* \(n = 40\) (sample size)

\[
SE = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx \frac{1.4}{6.3249} \approx 0.2215
\]

So the standard deviation (standard error) of the null‑hypothesis test is **≈ 0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test. That likely refers to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis? The standard error is sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test". Usually we compute the standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That is sigma/sqrt(n). But we don't know population sigma; we have sample sigma 1.4. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2215. So answer ~0.2215.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the t-statistic is sqrt((n-1)/n)? Actually t-statistic distribution has variance n/(n-2) for df=n-1? Wait: For t distribution with df = n-1, variance = df/(df-2) if df>2. So variance = (n-1)/(n-3). But that's for t distribution. But the question: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6." They might want the standard error of the mean difference: sqrt((s^2/n)+(sigma^2/N))? But no.

Better interpret: They want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That is the standard error: s / sqrt(n). So answer ~0.2215.

We can also compute the t-statistic: (98.2-98.6)/(1.4/sqrt(40)) = -0.4/0.2215 = -1.805. But they didn't ask for t-statistic.

Thus answer: ~0.2215.
